Traffic and Pedestrian Data

Tiasia Saunders

2026-06/01

Chicago Police Department versus other Illinois Law Enforcement Agencies Correlation with the Veil of Darkness

  • Pitch: Is Racial Bias in Traffic Stops a Chicago Problem or a Statewide Problem?

    • Using four years of Illinois traffic stop data from 2021 to 2024, I want to examine whether racial disparities in traffic stops extend beyond the Chicago Police Department to suburban and downstate Illinois law enforcement agencies. While CPD has faced significant scrutiny, especially since the fatal shooting of Dexter Reed, a 26-year-old Black man who was shot and killed in 2024 by the Chicago Police Department during a shootout between him and officers, smaller departments across Illinois operate with far less oversight and have received almost no data-driven accountability reporting.
    • By examining this through the veil of darkness lens, which controls for visibility conditions to isolate racial bias in stop decisions, across multiple Illinois agencies, I can determine whether this is a Chicago-specific failure or a statewide structural problem. If suburban departments, county sheriffs, and state police show the same pattern as CPD, that fundamentally re-frames the conversation around racial bias in Illinois policing and raises urgent questions about what oversight, if any, exists for the departments that fly under the radar.
    • While racial disparities in policing have been documented nationally, most public attention in Illinois focuses on the Chicago Police Department. If similar patterns appear across suburban, county, and state law enforcement agencies, it would suggest that racial bias is not isolated to one department but may be embedded throughout Illinois policing. This matters because many of these agencies receive far less public scrutiny, media coverage, and oversight despite conducting thousands of traffic stops each year.

  • Veil of Darkness Explanation:

    • It is a statistical methodology, created by Jeffrey Grogger and Greg Ridgeway in 2006, that is used to test for racial bias in traffic stops
    • It compares daytime stops to nighttime stops, relying on the hypothesis that at nighttime, natural darkness masks a driver’s race, which prevents racially biased officers from profiling them
    • The theory: if racial profiling exists, there should be a higher percentage of minority drivers stopped during daylight hours when officers can easily identify race, compared to nighttime hours when the ‘veil of darkness’ conceals the person’s race
    • Daytime: 6 a.m. to 5 p.m.
    • Nighttime: 10 p.m. to 4 a.m.
    • Excluded transition hours: 4 a.m.–5:59 a.m. and 5 p.m.–9:59 p.m.

  • Proposed Methodology: (How will I get the evidence needed to prove or disprove my hypothesis)

    • Will be looking at the racial breakdown of traffic stops across all Illinois law enforcement agencies, including CPD, to determine if there is a racial disparity in who gets stopped the most.
    • So analysis will be done on traffic_24 (all other Illinois law enforcement agencies traffic enforcement data) and traffic_CPD_24 (Chicago Police Department traffic enforcement data) to determine if there is a racial disparity in both CPD and the other Illinois law enforcement agencies, and then comparing the two to see if there is a similar pattern in both data sets.

  • Veil of Darkness: Will be determining racial bias through looking at the two sets of time ranges, the day and the night, to examine whether there is an obvious decrease in the amount of Black or brown people who are stopped at night due to the lack of visibility Suspicion Threshold: Will be looking at the resulting actions of stops after the initial traffic stop to determine whether there is a drastic disparity between how Black/brown versus white people are treated during a traffic stop

  • Will be looking at whether police officers have sufficient or suspected reason to search for evidence, and whether the ‘hit rate’ (that the officers do find something illegal) for minorities is relatively lower than their white counterparts or around the same, to determine if the threshold is equal for both

  • Will be examining racial disparities in the initial reason for the stop, and then the resulting actions of the stop (citation, written warning, verbal warning) to determine if there is a disparity there as well

  • Data Process Workflow:

  • So, I have downloaded the 16 (four per year from 2021-2024) datasets into my .rmd file and have begun preliminary analysis on it to see what I am working with

  • For the sake of time, I will be performing the analysis on just the 2024 traffic data. Might, look at pedestrian due to curiosity if time permits.

  • I have added the 2020 Census (let me know if there is a better source that could be used for this data) racial population makeup to my RMD.file to be able to calculate the per capita rates to determine which race is truly most impacted by traffic stops

  • I plan to determine the racial discrimination through three factors:

  • The veil of darkness angle

  • Examining the breakdown of the driver’s race, reason for the stop, and the result of the stop to determine if there are disparities there

  • Examining the reason for stop and hit rates (whether officers find something illegal during a search) for minorities versus white people to determine if there is a disparity in the suspicion threshold for minorities versus white people)

  • Hypothesis:

    • I suspect that I will find a pattern within the broader Illinois as a whole, that most of the law enforcement agencies (including CPD) tend to stop Black or minority race people more often in the daytime than at night, due to being able to identify the race in the daytime. Additionally, I suspect that there is a racial disparity between the initial reasoning for the traffic stop and the potential search and overall conclusion of the stop (citation, written warning, or verbal warning) between minority and white drivers.

  • Potential Problems with the Hypothesis/ Core Arguments:

  • Quick (two sentences) overview of what the story is about:

  • If racial disparities exist across Illinois agencies regardless of location or department size, it would suggest that concerns about biased policing extend far beyond Chicago and may require broader statewide accountability measures.

  • The Why:

    • If racial disparities exist across Illinois agencies regardless of location or department size, it would suggest that concerns about biased policing extend far beyond Chicago and may require broader statewide accountability measures.

  • Target Audience:

    • Illinois residents and drivers
    • Communities disproportionately affected by traffic enforcement
    • Police Department officials/ law enforcement officers
    • Policymakers and criminal justice reform advocates
    • Local government officials and police oversight bodies

  • Three Potential Interviewees:

    • A person impacted by racial discrimination during a traffic stop
    • Plan to look on social media for stories on TikTok, Reddit, or Instagram to be able to find an individual for this
    • A representative from the Illinois Department of Transportation or Illinois State Police familiar with statewide traffic stop reporting requirements.
    • A civil rights attorney, policing researcher, or advocate who studies racial disparities in traffic enforcement.

  • Data Records:

    • I already received the data from the Investigative Project on Race and Equity, and it includes data from 2021-2024. Each year has four datasets, two from the Chicago Police Department data (traffic and pedestrian data) and two from other Illinois police departments’ data (traffic and pedestrian data.
    • I will be bringing in the 2020 Census Illinois population racial breakdown data to be able to calculate the per capita rates to be able to have a true reflection of who police traffic stops impact the most.

  • Visual Ideas:

    • Statewide map showing racial disparities in stop rates by agency.
    • Bar chart comparing racial composition of daytime versus nighttime stops.
    • Scatterplot comparing stop disparities and search hit rates by department.
    • An interactive dashboard allowing readers to compare agencies.
    • Timeline showing trends in racial disparities from 2021 to 2024

  • Impact:

    • This project could reveal whether racial disparities in traffic stops are a problem across Illinois, not just within the Chicago Police Department. The findings could help inform conversations about police accountability and bring attention to departments that conduct thousands of traffic stops each year but rarely face public scrutiny.

  • Resources:

    • https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2020/05/veil-darkness-reduces-racial-bias-traffic-stops
    • https://5harad.com/papers/100M-stops.pdf

Data Tables Definitions
  • traffic_x: data of traffic stops happening under other agencies, other than Chicago police department
  • traffic_CPD_x: data of traffic stops happening under Chicago police department
  • pedestrian_redacted_x: data of pedestrian stops happening under other agencies, other than Chicago police department
  • pedestrian_CPD_x: data of pedestrian stops happening under Chicago police department
Data that I am using for this analysis:
  • traffic_2024: data of other law enforcement agencies happening under different agencies in Illinois
  • traffic_CPD_2024: data of traffic stops happening under Chicago police department

  • So, for the sake of my analysis, I am using 2024 Chicago Police Department and other Illinois law enforcement agencies. I am attempting to find racial disparities through the per capita of 100k people in total stops, reason for stop, and result of stop. Additionally, I am categorizing time frames (10 pm - 4 am = nighttime, 6 am - 5 pm = daytime) to examine the disparities in the data through the veil of darkness angle.

Preliminary Basic Analysis
  • Redefining my columns by their associated meaning according to the traffic stop data dictionary, so I can have a better understanding of the data and be able to do more analysis on it.
# re coding the race and gender numerical values into what they stand for according to the traffic stop data dictionary 

traffic_CPD_24 <- traffic_CPD_24 |>
  mutate(
    sex = recode(as.character(drsex),
      "1" = "Male",
      "2" = "Female",
      "3" = "Non-Binary", 
      "9" = "Unknown"
    ),
    race = recode(as.character(drrace),
      "1" = "White",
      "2" = "Black",
      "3" = "American Indian",
      "4" = "Hispanic",
      "5" = "Asian",
      "6" = "NHPI"
    ),
    vehicle_search = recode(as.character(vehsrchcond), 
      "1" = "Yes",  
      "2" = "No" 
    ), 
    vehicle_drugs_found = recode(as.character(vehdrugs),
      "0" = "Not applicable",
      "1" = "Yes",
      "2" = "No"
    ), 
    reason_for_stop = recode(as.character(reasstop), 
      "1" = "Moving Violation", 
      "2" = "Equipment", 
      "3" = "License Plate/ Registration",
      "4" = "Commercial Vehicle"
    ), 
    result_of_stop = recode(as.character(resstop),
      "1" = "Citation",
      "2" = "Written Warning", 
      "3" = "Verbal Warning (stop card)"
    )
  )

gender_race_CPD_24 <- gender_race_CPD_24 |>
  arrange(desc(n)) |>
  mutate(
    highlight = if_else(row_number() <= 3, "Top 3", "Other"),
    group = paste(sex, race)
  )

ggplot(
  gender_race_CPD_24,
  aes(
    x = reorder(group, n),
    y = n,
    fill = highlight
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  
  geom_text(
    aes(label = comma(n)),
    hjust = -0.1,
    size = 3
  ) +
  
  coord_flip() +
  
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Top 3" = "#B22222",
      "Other" = "gray70"
    )
  ) +
  
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = comma,
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .15))
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Chicago Police Department Traffic stops by race and sex",
    subtitle = "Top three race-gender groups highlighted",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of stops",
    caption = "Source: Chicago Police Department • Graphic by Tiasia Saunders"
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

  • In 2024, there were 206,148 men who were involved in a CPD traffic stop, while 86,591 women were stopped, and 4ll non-binary people were stopped.
  • As for race, in descending order Black people were stopped 130,938 times, followed by Hispanic/ Latino with 101,891 stops, and then white people were stopped 43,304 times.
  • When broken down by gender and race, it was found that the top three gender/racial demographics who were stopped by CPD in 2024 were Black men with 85,522 stops, Hispanic men with 76,917 stops, and Black women with 45,225 stops.

timeline_monthly <- traffic_CPD_24 |>
  mutate(month = floor_date(as.Date(datestop), "month")) |>
  count(month)

max_stops <- max(timeline_monthly$n)

ggplot(timeline_monthly, aes(x = month, y = n)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +

  geom_vline(
    xintercept = as.Date("2024-03-21"),
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "red"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "label",
    x = as.Date("2024-03-21"),
    y = max_stops * 0.9,
    label = "Dexter Reed fatal\nshooting incident",
    size = 2
  ) +

  geom_vline(
    xintercept = as.Date("2024-08-21"),
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "red"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "label",
    x = as.Date("2024-08-21"),
    y = max_stops * 0.75,
    label = "Injustice Watch investigation:\nNearly 200,000 undocumented arrests",
    size = 2
  ) +

  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "1 month",
    date_labels = "%b"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::comma
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Chicago Police Department traffic stops by month, 2024",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of stops",
    caption = "Source: Chicago Police Department • Graphic by Tiasia Saunders"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 1, size = 8, color = "gray40")
  )

- So, I looked into an explanation as to why there was a steady decrease of traffic stops by the CPD in 2024, so once looking it up I found this article which explained that there were 210,622 undocumented traffic stops in 2024, despite a 2003 law requiring them to document every traffic stop - In addition, the Dexter Reed incident in which a 26-year old Black man died at the result of a shootout incident between him and policemen in late March of 2024, may have resulted in heavier scrutiny due to advocacy groups and civil rights lawsuits. - The incident had stemmed from a seatbelt violation traffic stop

At first glance, it looks like white people are being stopped more than their minority counterparts, but as I hypothesized, I believe this is due to the population size of white people being very big in the state of Illinois. So, I am now going to account for per capital calculations with both the CPD to ensure that minorities are the most likely to be stopped and see if it lies true for the other local law enforcement agencies.

Per Capital Calculations to get a true reflection of the data, I need to account for population size when looking at the number of stops by race.

##  REDO THIS CHUNK calculating for the per capital of total stops by race 
 census_race <- tibble(
  race = c(
    "White",
    "Black",
    "American Indian",
    "Asian",
    "NHPI",
    "Hispanic"
  ),
  population_number = c(
    7472751,
    1775612,
    16561,
    747280,
    2959,
    2337410
  )
)

per_capita_CPD_race <- traffic_CPD_24 |>
  count(race, name = "total_stops") |>
  left_join(census_race, by = "race") |>
  mutate(
    stops_per_100k = round((total_stops / population_number) * 100000, 1)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(stops_per_100k))

per_capita_CPD_race

## 4 Hispanic             101891           2337410          4359.
## 5 Asian                 14139            747280          1892.
## 6 White                 43304           7472751           580.
census_race <- census_race |>
  mutate(
    race = recode(race,

    )
  )

Veil of Darkness Element (Very Basic Level)
## categorizing my time frames in my 2024 CPD traffic + other traffic datasets 

traffic_CPD_24 <- traffic_CPD_24 |>
  mutate(
    stop_hour = hour(timestop),
    light_period = case_when(
      stop_hour >= 6 & stop_hour < 17 ~ "Daytime",
      stop_hour >= 22 | stop_hour < 4 ~ "Nighttime",
      TRUE ~ "Excluded transition hours"
    )
  )

traffic_CPD_24 |>
  count(light_period)
## # A tibble: 3 × 2
##   light_period                   n
##   <chr>                      <int>
## 1 Daytime                   128683
## 2 Excluded transition hours  92618
## 3 Nighttime                  71849
traffic_CPD_24 <- traffic_CPD_24 |>
  mutate(
    race = recode(
      race,
      "American Indian" = "AIAN"
    )
  )

veil_race_CPD_24 <- traffic_CPD_24 |>
  filter(light_period != "Excluded transition hours") |>
  count(light_period, race) |>
  group_by(light_period) |>
  mutate(percent = n / sum(n) * 100) |>
  ungroup()

veil_race_CPD_24
## # A tibble: 12 × 4
##    light_period race         n percent
##    <chr>        <chr>    <int>   <dbl>
##  1 Daytime      AIAN       536   0.417
##  2 Daytime      Asian     4408   3.43 
##  3 Daytime      Black    61809  48.0  
##  4 Daytime      Hispanic 40745  31.7  
##  5 Daytime      NHPI       353   0.274
##  6 Daytime      White    20832  16.2  
##  7 Nighttime    AIAN       824   1.15 
##  8 Nighttime    Asian     5440   7.57 
##  9 Nighttime    Black    29433  41.0  
## 10 Nighttime    Hispanic 26550  37.0  
## 11 Nighttime    NHPI       250   0.348
## 12 Nighttime    White     9352  13.0
veil_race_CPD_24 <- traffic_CPD_24 |>
  mutate(
    stop_hour = hour(timestop),
    light_period = case_when(
      stop_hour >= 6 & stop_hour < 17 ~ "☀ Daytime",
      stop_hour >= 22 | stop_hour < 4 ~ "☾ Nighttime",
      TRUE ~ "Excluded transition hours"
    )
  ) |>
  filter(light_period != "Excluded transition hours") |>
  count(light_period, race) |>
  group_by(light_period) |>
  mutate(
    percent = n / sum(n) * 100,
    race_ordered = reorder_within(race, percent, light_period),
    highlight = if_else(race %in% c("Black", "Hispanic"), "Highlighted", "Other")
  ) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(
  veil_race_CPD_24,
  aes(
    x = race_ordered,
    y = percent,
    fill = highlight
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(percent, 1), "%")),
    hjust = -0.1,
    size = 3
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  facet_wrap(~ light_period, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_reordered() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Highlighted" = "#B22222",
      "Other" = "gray75"
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_percent(scale = 1),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Racial breakdown of CPD traffic stops during\n daylight and nighttime hours",
    subtitle = "Daytime includes 6 a.m.– 5 p.m.; nighttime includes 10 p.m.– 4 a.m.",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Share of stops",
    caption = "Source: Illinois traffic stop data • Graphic by Tiasia Saunders"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 7, color = "gray40", hjust = 1),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  )

- Black drivers accounted for the largest share of Chicago traffic stops during both daytime (48.0%) and nighttime (41.0%) hours. - Hispanic drivers’ share increased from 31.7% during the day to 37.0% at night. - White drivers accounted for 16.2% of daytime stops and 13.0% of nighttime stops. - At first I was a little confused, but then I realized the racial distribution of stops in Chicago differs substantially from statewide Illinois traffic-stop patterns, where White drivers make up the majority of stops.

    percent = n / sum(n) * 100,
    race_ordered = reorder_within(driver_race, percent, light_period),
    highlight = if_else(driver_race %in% c("Black", "Hispanic"), "Highlight", "Other")
  ) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(veil_race, aes(x = race_ordered, y = percent, fill = highlight)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(percent, 1), "%")),
    hjust = -0.1,
    size = 3
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  facet_wrap(~ light_period, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_reordered() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Highlight" = "#B22222",
      "Other" = "gray75"
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_percent(scale = 1),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Racial breakdown of traffic stops during daylight and nighttime hours",
    subtitle = "Daytime: 6 a.m.–5 p.m.; Nighttime: 10 p.m.–4 a.m.",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Share of stops",
    caption = "Source: Illinois traffic stop data • Graphic by Tiasia Saunders"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 7, color = "gray40", hjust = 1),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  )

  • During the day, Black drivers account for 18.8 percent of stops and at night they account for 27.1 percent of stops
    • That’s an increase of 8.3 percentage points, which is a 44 percent increase in the share of stops that Black drivers account for at night compared to the day
  • On the other hand, white drivers fall from 58.1 percent of stops during the day to 46.8 percent at night
    • That’s a decrease of 11.3 percentage points, which is a 19.5 percent decrease in the share of stops that white drivers account for at night compared to the day

Conclusion (thus far):

  • CPD Traffic stops by racial disparities breakdown:
    • Black drivers represented the largest share of traffic stops during both daytime and nighttime hours, accounting for 48.0% of stops during the day and 41.0% at night, while Hispanic drivers’ share increased from 31.7% during the day to 37.0% at night, and White drivers accounted for 16.2% of daytime stops and 13.0% of nighttime stops.
  • Illinois Traffic stops by other law enforcement agencies:
    • Black drivers represented a larger share of traffic stops during nighttime hours than during daytime hours, increasing from 18.8% of stops to 27.1%, while White drivers’ share declined from 58.1% to 46.8%.
  • Per capital calculations:
    • CPD traffic stop rates were highest among NHPI and American Indian residents, though those rates are based on much smaller population counts (should I take them out). Among larger racial groups, Black residents had the highest stop rate, with about 7,374 stops per 100,000 residents, compared with 580 per 100,000 white residents.
    • Illinois state traffic stop rates were highest among NHPI and American Indian residents, though those rates are based on much smaller population counts. Among larger racial groups, Black residents had the highest stop rate, with about 7,374 stops per 100,000 residents, compared with 580 per 100,000 white residents.
    • As for the general Illinois law enforcement agencies data, Among larger racial groups, Black residents had the highest stop rate, with about 7,374 stops per 100,000 residents, compared with 580 per 100,000 white residents.
  • Overall, I would say the veil of darkness element does seem to be supported by the data, as there is a noticeable increase in the share of stops that Black drivers account for at night compared to the day, and a noticeable decrease in the share of stops that white drivers account for at night compared to the day. However, I would say that this is not a definitive conclusion, as there could be other factors at play that are contributing to these trends, such as differences in driving patterns or law enforcement practices during different times of the day.
  • If I had the opportunity to expand on this project, I would definitely to strengthen the veil of darkness angle.
  • Overall, I would say that the data does seem to support the idea that there are racial disparities in traffic stops, and that these disparities are more pronounced during nighttime hours, which is consistent with the veil of darkness theory. However, I would also say that there are likely other factors at play that are contributing to these trends, and that further research would be needed to fully understand the underlying causes of these disparities.
